Week 8 · Modules 9 to 11 · five days · about 6 hours in total

Claude asks for a tool. Your workflow runs it, and the number comes out right.

In Week 7 you attached tools to an agent and n8n did the plumbing. This week I open the hood. You will work in the Anthropic Console, write a tool schema by hand and watch Claude ask for it, give an agent a retrieval tool, and then build the hardest agent in the course: one that reads messy finance spreadsheets and gets every number exactly right, because the arithmetic happens in a tool and never in the model's head. Five short days, then two labs on Day 5.

      Day 1 · about 40 minutes
      
Where the API lives: the Anthropic Console

      
Everything you build from here on calls Claude through the API, and the Console is where that account is managed. By the end of today you will have a workspace with a spending limit, a key stored where it belongs, you will know what a 429 means, and you will have seen the exact request Workbench sends. Every widget on this page is live; poke it.

A workspace is a budget with its own keys

        
Most companies hand out purchase cards with a monthly limit, one per team, and nobody writes the card number on a sticky note. The Anthropic Console works the same way. It lives at console.anthropic.com and it is the API side of Claude. You chatted in claude.ai during Weeks 1 to 4; here you set up the account that n8n and your own code will call.

        
The unit of organisation is the workspace. Each one has its own API keys, its own spending limit, its own rate limits and its own usage page, so make at least two: one called Course, for everything you build in these ten weeks, and one for the first real pilot at work. When the pilot's bill arrives you will know exactly what it cost, and when a course experiment runs away it cannot touch the pilot's budget.

        
API keys belong to a workspace. The Console shows a new key once, at the moment you create it, and never again, so copy it straight into n8n's Credentials store, not into a node, a chat or a shared document. Give each place that uses Claude its own key, named for the place: n8n-cloud, laptop, finance-pilot. If one leaks you revoke that one, within a minute, and nothing else breaks. A leaked key is not a disaster if you can revoke it. It is a disaster if the same key is pasted into eleven places.

        
Spending limits are the part people skip. Set a monthly cap on each workspace before the first request. When it is reached the API refuses new requests with an error rather than quietly running up a bill. Press Simulate a month on the left and watch the pilot workspace hit its cap on day four. The hub's rules asked you to set a limit on day one of the course; if you have not, today is the day.

        
The syllabus says "Workspaces, Projects". In the Console the unit is the workspace. Projects are the claude.ai feature from Week 3, a folder of files and instructions for chatting, and the two are not connected. I have watched people hunt for a Projects tab in the Console for ten minutes. Members and their roles (admin, developer, billing) sit one level up, on the organisation.

        
One workspace per purpose, one key per place, a spending limit before the first request.

Why the API answered 429

        
Picture a customer service line that can take fifty calls a minute. The fifty-first caller hears a busy tone, not a wrong answer. Rate limits work like that. Every workspace has, for each model, a ceiling on requests per minute and on input and output tokens per minute, and the ceilings depend on your usage tier. A new account starts low, and the limits rise as you spend and as the account ages.

        
When you cross a ceiling the API answers with status 429 and an error typed rate_limit_error, together with a retry-after header that says how long to wait. Nothing is wrong with your prompt or your key. The SDKs retry a 429 on their own with a growing pause, and in n8n you turn on the node's Retry On Fail setting with a wait between tries. In a course workspace you will mostly meet 429s when you send a burst, for example a test with twenty items that all reach the model at once.

        
The widget on the left is a token bucket, which is roughly how the limits behave: each request takes tokens out, and the bucket refills through the minute. Send one request and it passes. Send a burst at Tier 1 and the bucket empties, so the last requests bounce. Switch to Tier 2 and the same burst sails through. Where the picture is too simple: the refill is continuous, not a reset at the top of each minute, and output tokens have their own ceiling, so one long answer can use up a budget that a short input never touched.

        
Three errors look alike to a tired person and mean different things. A 401 means the key is wrong or revoked. A 429 means too much in one minute. A 400 with a billing message means the spending limit from the last concept was reached, or the prepaid balance ran out. Read the status code first; it tells you which page of the Console to open.

        
A 429 means "too much in one minute", not "bad prompt". Wait, retry, or raise the tier.

Workbench shows you the exact request

        
Before a new analyst sends a first email to a client, you read a few drafts over their shoulder. Workbench is that for the API. It is a page in the Console where you write a system prompt and a user message, pick a model, attach tools and press run, with no workflow and no code. The reply appears, and so does the thing that matters more this week: the exact request the API received.

        
That request is a small JSON object with a handful of fields. model names the model, max_tokens caps the reply, system carries your standing instructions, messages holds the conversation, and tools, when you add any, holds the schemas we write tomorrow. Press Get code in Workbench and it turns the same request into Python or TypeScript you could run. When n8n calls Claude for you next week it sends this shape and nothing more exotic.

        
The model picker is where names bite. As I write, the everyday model is claude-sonnet-5-5, with claude-haiku-5-5 for cheap high-volume steps and claude-opus-5-5 where quality matters most. The syllabus this course is built from says "Claude 3.5 Sonnet", which is two generations old. Names change every few months. The habit that lasts is to pick the current Sonnet-class model and to glance at the pricing page, because every Workbench run costs real money, charged to the workspace. The mock on the left estimates it: a few hundred tokens at Sonnet prices is a fraction of a cent.

        
Try it. Tick "attach the calculate_kpi tool" and open the Response tab. With no tool, the model answers the margin question from its head and hedges with "about 41 percent", because it is predicting digits. With the tool attached, the same question comes back not as an answer but as a request to call the tool. That is the whole of tomorrow.

        
Workbench is the API with a face. Whatever you see there is exactly what n8n sends later.

      Day 2 · about 50 minutes
      
What n8n did for you in Week 7, done by hand

      
Two ideas today: the four messages that make up one tool call, and the schema Claude reads to decide which tool to ask for. By the end you can read a tool_use block, you will have written a schema that scores five out of five, and you will have made Claude ask for a tool in Workbench.

    


    
    

      

        

          
          
          
        

        

        
The messages array as your workflow resends it on every turn. Token counts are illustrative.0 messages0 tokens

      

      

        
Claude asks, your workflow runs, the result goes back

        
When a manager asks an analyst for the quarter's gross margin, a good analyst does not guess. She says "one moment", opens the spreadsheet, runs the formula and reads the number back. Tool calling is the API version of that pause. In Week 7 the AI Agent node hid it from you. Here it is in the open, as four messages.

        
First, your workflow sends the request: the conversation so far plus a tools list, each tool described as a schema. Second, Claude answers not with prose but with a tool_use block: the tool's name, the inputs it wants and an id, and the response is marked stop_reason: "tool_use", which means "I am waiting". Third, your workflow runs the tool, whatever that means for you (a Code node, a Sheets lookup, an HTTP request), and sends the output back as a tool_result carrying the same id. Fourth, Claude reads the result and writes the answer, now marked end_turn. Step through the array on the left and watch it grow.

        
Notice who does what. Claude never runs anything. It writes a request, in a shape your code can parse, and waits. That is why tool calling is safe to put near real systems: the model never holds your database password or your Gmail login, your workflow can check every input before acting, and it can refuse. Switch the scenario to "the tool fails" to see the other half of the contract. You send the result back with is_error set, and Claude explains or asks instead of inventing a number.

        
Where the analyst analogy breaks: she remembers the conversation; Claude does not. The API is stateless, so every turn your workflow resends the whole messages array, tool results included, and each of them lands on the desk from Week 1 and costs tokens. A tool that returns 2,000 rows puts 2,000 rows in the context window. Return what the model needs, not what the database has. One more detail: Claude may ask for several tools in one message. Run them all and return all the results in one message, in the same order.

        
Server-side tools. Anthropic also runs a few tools on its own side, such as web search and code execution. You declare them in the same tools list and the results arrive inside the response. Everything you build in n8n this week is the other kind: your side runs it, and your side is responsible for it.

        
Four messages: request with tools, tool_use, tool_result, answer. Claude writes the request; your workflow does the work.

A schema is a prompt in disguise

        
Think about how HR writes a job description: a title, a paragraph on what the role does and when you would call on that person, and a list of what they need to be given to do the work. A tool schema has exactly those three parts, and Claude reads it the way a manager reads a job description when deciding whom to ask.

        
The name is a verb and a noun in snake_case: calculate_kpi, load_sheet, flag_anomaly. The description is a paragraph in plain English, and it is the part that does the work: what the tool does, when to use it, and when not to. The input_schema is JSON Schema, which sounds technical and is mostly bookkeeping: each input gets a type (string, number, array, boolean), a one-line description and a place in the required list. Write all three as English sentences first. The JSON on the left is generated from them, and in Workbench you type the same things into a form.

        
The description is where agents go wrong. "Gets data" gives Claude nothing to decide with, so it guesses from the name. "Return all rows from one named sheet of the uploaded workbook. Use when the user asks for data that has not been loaded yet. Do not use to calculate anything; call calculate_kpi for that" tells it when and when not, and names the neighbour it might confuse. Half of Week 7's debugging was rewriting descriptions. Now you know the shape they should take, and the linter on the left checks the five things I check.

        
Where this breaks: no description can rescue two tools that overlap. If load_sheet and get_data both exist, Claude will pick one of them for the wrong reasons. Keep each tool narrow, keep the set small (three to seven for one agent) and make the boundaries explicit in the text. A newer option, strict mode, makes the API guarantee that the inputs match your schema exactly. It does not help the model choose; it only fills the form correctly once the choice is made.

        
Name, description, inputs. The description is a prompt: say what, when, and when not.

      Day 3 · about 55 minutes
      
How n8n turns a node into a tool, and a vector store into one too

      
Yesterday's four messages and schema, seen from inside n8n. By the end you can point at the n8n setting behind every field of a tool schema, and you will have given an agent a retrieval tool over your Week 5 documents.

What n8n does with the schema

        
If you have ever set up a supplier in a procurement system, you know the feeling of filling in fields that some other system will read later: the legal name, the bank details, the payment terms. When you attached a Gmail or Sheets node to the AI Agent in Week 7, you were filling in a tool schema without seeing it. n8n reads the node, writes yesterday's JSON from it, and sends it in the tools list.

        
The mapping is nearly one to one. The node's name becomes the tool's name, with spaces turned into underscores. The node's Description field becomes the description, and for app nodes it has a dropdown: "Set automatically" uses n8n's generic text, which is the weak default, and "Set manually" lets you write the what, when and when not. Any parameter you switch to "Let the model define this parameter" becomes a property in input_schema. Under the hood n8n writes an expression, $fromAI('kpi_type', 'One of margin, growth_rate, average, total', 'string'), whose three arguments are the property's name, description and type. Everything you fill in yourself stays fixed and invisible to the model.

        
Then the loop from yesterday runs. n8n receives the tool_use block, executes the node with the model's inputs in place of the $fromAI expressions, and returns the node's output as the tool_result. Two special tools matter this week. The Code Tool runs JavaScript or Python you supply, with an input schema you declare, and it is how the Analytics Agent will do its arithmetic. The Call n8n Workflow Tool turns a whole sub-workflow into one tool, its trigger's inputs becoming the schema, which is how you build specialists.

        
Where it breaks: a node with twenty parameters becomes a twenty-field schema if you let the model define all of them, and the model will fill in the ones it does not understand. Let it decide only what it should decide, two or three fields, and fix the rest yourself. And n8n's automatic descriptions are written for every user on earth, so they say nothing about your sheets or your rules. Click the four parts on the left to see each API field next to the n8n setting that produces it.

        
Labels move. n8n ships a release most weeks. The field names here are from the 1.x series of late 2026; if your screen says something slightly different, look for the idea (a description the model reads, parameters the model fills) rather than the exact words.

        
n8n writes the schema from the node: the name, the Description field, the $fromAI inputs. Fix the description and you fix most of the agent.

      

    


    
    

      

        
        

          
          
        

        
Ingest: three pages become twelve chunks, then vectors in the store.

        

      

      

        
Retrieval is a tool the agent decides to call

        
When a colleague asks whether taxis from the airport are claimable, you do not recite the expenses policy from memory. You open it, find the paragraph and read it out. In Week 5 you did the same for Claude by hand: chunk, embed, store, search, paste the chunks into the prompt. n8n has a node for every one of those steps, and it can hand the search itself to the agent as a tool.

        
The ingest side is a pipeline you run once, or whenever the documents change. A Default Data Loader reads the files, a Text Splitter cuts them into chunks (start at 500 tokens with an overlap of 50), an Embeddings sub-node turns each chunk into a vector, and a Vector Store node in insert mode saves vectors and text together. The store is your choice: Qdrant or Pinecone in the cloud, which persist and need credentials, or n8n's Simple Vector Store, which lives in memory and is perfect for a lab. Switch between them on the left and watch what changes: nothing in the pipeline, only where the vectors sleep.

        
The retrieval side is a tool. Attach a Vector Store Tool to the AI Agent, point it at the same store with the same embeddings model, and give it a description: "Search the company policy handbook. Use for questions about leave, expenses, refunds and security." Now the agent decides when it needs facts, calls the tool, gets back the top few chunks as the tool_result and answers from them, naming the source. Week 5's RAG loop has become one tool call among others, and the agent can combine it with a calculation or an email in the same run.

        
Where it breaks, twice. A vector store always returns its nearest chunks, even for "what is the capital of Peru?", so the agent must be told: if the retrieved text does not answer the question, say so. And insert and query must use the same embeddings model, or nothing matches and nobody tells you; you simply get odd chunks back and a confident answer built on them.

        
Claude does not produce embeddings. The Embeddings sub-node uses a different provider: Cohere, Google, OpenAI, Mistral, or a local model through Ollama. That is normal. Turning text into vectors and reasoning over text are two different jobs, and the embedding model is small and cheap by comparison.

        
Ingest is a pipeline you run once. Retrieval is a tool the agent calls when it needs facts, and each call costs tokens like any other.

Numbers must come from a tool, never from the model's head

      
Week 1's arithmetic failures return, with the fix. By the end you can explain why every number in a report must pass through code, you will have watched a tool catch the model's slip, and you will have had Claude write a Code node for messy sheets without writing a line yourself.

The model proposes. Code verifies.

        

        
Every number in an executive summary should take the right-hand path.slips caught: 0 of 0 runs

      

      

        
Week 1's arithmetic failures come back, with a fix

        
In Week 1 you pasted 25 invoice amounts into a chat, asked for the total and got a confident number that was wrong. Nothing about the model has changed since. It still reads numbers as tokens, still predicts digits instead of carrying them, and still cannot tell a right sum from a wrong one, because both feel like high-probability text from the inside.

        
What has changed is that you now have tools. Give the agent a calculator or a Code tool and the rule becomes simple: the model decides what to compute, the tool computes it, and the model reports the tool's number word for word. On the left, the model proposes a total and one line of code verifies it. Set the size to five numbers and the model is usually right. Set it to forty and it almost never is. Small sums look fine, and that is exactly what makes long ones dangerous: the habit of trusting the small ones carries over.

        
This is why the syllabus calls what you build this week a Math and Analytics Agent. The maths is not the model's job. Its job is to understand the question, pick the formula, map the columns, call the tool and write the summary. The MIT xPRO course, Designing and Building AI Products and Services, says in its module on business applications that the basic requirements for AI in a company come down to two things: people and data. Here the data is a messy spreadsheet, and the people are the finance colleague who knows that "Qty" means units sold and that March's "n/a" means the supplier never sent the invoice. The model cannot know your conventions. A person writes them into the system prompt.

        
Where the fix breaks: a tool is only as right as its inputs. If the model passes the wrong column to the calculator, the code computes the wrong thing to the cent. So the manual check on Day 5 does not go away. The tool removes one source of error, the arithmetic, and the log you will read on Day 5 catches the other, the choice of inputs.

        
The model proposes, the tool computes, the model reports the tool's number word for word.

      

    


    
    

      

        

          

          Harbor Lane Coffee · Q1.xlsx
        

        

        

          
          
          
          
        

        

        
    
        
    
        
    
        
    Three monthly sheets and an expenses sheet, with the three classic defects. The totals are computed live by the code you can show.
    
      
    
      
    
        
    Messy sheets in, KPIs out, without writing the code yourself
    
        
    Every finance team has that workbook. Three monthly tabs, one of which someone renamed in February, a blank row where a formula used to be, and an "n/a" sitting in a column of numbers. A person opens it and quietly fixes all three before adding anything up. An agent has to be told to, and that is the whole design of the Analytics Agent.
    
        
    The workflow is short. A Form Trigger or Webhook receives the file, Extract from File turns each sheet into an item, and the AI Agent takes over with three kinds of tool: a Code tool for arithmetic, the three tools you design in Lab 4.1, and a Structured Output Parser so the final report comes out as fields rather than prose. The order of work matters more than the nodes. Normalise first: map every sheet's columns onto one canonical set, skip blank rows, and treat anything non-numeric as missing and flagged, never as zero. Then compute, from the normalised table only. Then write, using the computed numbers and the list of flags.
    
        
    You do not write the code. You describe it to Claude in plain English, paste what it writes into the Code node, run it and read the output. If it errors, you paste the error back and get a corrected version. Press Normalise on the left to see the mapping the agent should make, then Compute to see what the Code node returns: revenue 184,250.00, gross margin 41.00 percent, net profit 24,250.00 and two flags. Press "Show the code" and you will find thirty lines you can read even if you could not have written them.
    
        
    Where it breaks: mapping columns is itself a judgment. "COGS" is obviously cost of goods; "Amt" could be anything. The rule for the agent is to flag an ambiguous column rather than guess, and to exclude a non-numeric cell rather than invent a value, because a flagged gap is a question a person answers in a minute and an invented number is a mistake that travels into the CFO's summary. One habit from the MIT course's hierarchy of needs applies here: look at your data before you model it. Open every sheet yourself before you let the agent at them.
    
        
    Normalise, then compute, then write. The code does the middle step; the model does the first and last and flags whatever it could not fix.

      Day 5 · about 150 minutes

    Execution monitoring is decision tracing
    
        
    When an auditor asks how a number in the annual report was produced, "the spreadsheet said so" is not an answer. You show the cells, the formula and who changed what. An agent needs the same trail, and n8n keeps it for you. Every run leaves an execution: each node, what went in, what came out, and for the AI Agent node, with Return Intermediate Steps switched on, every tool call, its inputs, its result and the tokens it used. That is the context payload the syllabus talks about: the exact text the model had in front of it at each step.
    
        
    Reading a log is a skill with one rule. When the final number is wrong, do not reread the prompt and guess. Open the run, walk the steps in order, and find the first step where the wrong number appears. Everything after it inherits the error. On the left, the good run and the run with a bug are identical until step 5. In the good run the agent calls the Code tool and the margin is 41.00 percent. In the bad run there is no tool call: the model added the cost column in its head, got "about 95,900", and 48 percent travelled into a perfectly well-formed report. The output parser was happy. The number was wrong.
    
        
    The MIT xPRO course, Designing and Building AI Products and Services, has a name for this. In its module on business applications, Barbara Wixom of MIT's Center for Information Systems Research argues that companies which actually make money from AI build a capability she calls explanation, and that it shows up as four practices. Boundary setting: what the agent is allowed to decide, which for you is the tool list and the rule "never do arithmetic yourself". Value formation: which process improves and by how much, here a CFO summary in thirty seconds instead of a day. Decision tracing: understanding how inputs became outputs, which is exactly what the execution log gives you. Bias remediation: knowing how the system goes wrong in specific cases and how you fix it, which is your anomaly flags and the manual check. Execution monitoring is decision tracing in practice.
    
        
    In production you do not open every run by hand. The last node of the workflow appends one row per run to a log sheet: timestamp, steps, tokens, cost, the tools called and whether the result matched a check. The widget writes that row when the run finishes. Where logs fall short: they show what the model did, not why it chose it. The reasoning is not in the log unless you ask the model to write it out, so you also test with known answers. That is what the lab's validation step is, the eval habit from your Week 1 failure notebook applied to an agent.
    
        
    When the number is wrong, open the log and find the first step where it went wrong. That is decision tracing, and it is your audit trail.

    Lab 4.1 · tool-calling schemas in the Anthropic Workbench
    
      
      
        
    1. Design three tools on paper first, in plain English, before you touch Workbench. load_sheet returns the rows of one named sheet. calculate_kpi computes one KPI from numbers it is given (the Day 2 builder). flag_anomaly marks one value as unusual and records why. For each: what it does, when to use it, when not to, and its inputs with types.
      
          
      Starting schemas for load_sheet and flag_anomaly
      # load_sheet
name: load_sheet
description: Return all rows from one named sheet of the uploaded workbook.
  Use when the user asks for data that has not been loaded yet.
  Do not use to calculate anything; call calculate_kpi for that.
inputs:
  sheet_name (string, required, the exact tab name, such as "Mar")
  max_rows (number, optional, default 500)

# flag_anomaly
name: flag_anomaly
description: Mark one value as unusual and record why.
  Use when a value is negative where it cannot be, is more than 3x the
  typical value for its column, or is text in a number column.
  Do not use for ordinary month-to-month changes under 50 percent.
inputs:
  sheet_name (string, required)
  row (number, required, 1-based row number, header not counted)
  value (string, required, the value exactly as it appears)
  reason (string, required, one plain sentence)

      Check yourself
      
    Eight quick questions
    
      
    Pick an answer to see why it is right or wrong. Score 80 percent or more to pass. Nobody is watching; the point is to find out what did not stick.
    
    
    
    
    
    
    Think it through
    
    
    
      
    Who actually runs a tool: Claude or your workflow? Why does it matter for security?
    Your workflow runs it. Claude only returns a message that names the tool and its inputs, and then waits. That means Claude never holds your database password, your Gmail login or your API keys, and your code can check or refuse every input before anything happens in the world. A tool call is a request, not an action, which is why you can put an agent next to real systems and still sleep.
    
      
    Why must the agent's arithmetic go through a Code tool even though Claude can "do maths"?
    A language model predicts the next token, including digits. It is often right on small sums and quietly wrong on long ones, and it cannot tell the difference from the inside, because a right total and a wrong total both feel like fluent text. Code computes the exact answer every time. In a finance report one wrong digit costs more than the whole workflow, so the rule is absolute: the model picks the formula and the inputs, the tool does the arithmetic, the model quotes the result.
    
      
    Your agent reported margin as 48 percent and your spreadsheet says 41. Name three places in the pipeline where the difference could come from.
    Loading: a sheet with renamed columns mapped "Qty" or "COGS" to the wrong field, or the blank row and the "n/a" cell were dropped silently along with their revenue. Calculating: the model did the division itself instead of calling the Code tool, or passed the wrong list of values. Reporting: the parser accepted a rounded or mislabelled number, gross margin where you expected net, for example. The execution log tells you which, because the wrong number first appears at exactly one step.
    
      
    Your retrieval tool returned three chunks for "what is the capital of Peru?" and the agent answered from them. What went wrong, and which two fixes would you try?
    Nothing went wrong in the store; a vector store always returns its nearest chunks, however far away they are. The agent's mistake was to treat "nearest" as "relevant". First fix: a system-prompt rule that says if the retrieved text does not answer the question, say the documents do not cover it. Second fix: a sharper tool description that says what the handbook does and does not contain, so the agent does not call the tool for general knowledge in the first place. If odd chunks come back for on-topic questions too, check that insert and query use the same embeddings model.
